title: How the National Security Council Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the US National Security Council (NSC): why Congress created it in 1947 with the National Security Act (Truman signed it), how its structure of policy coordinating committees, deputies committee, and principals committee funnels issues up to the president, and how the National Security Advisor and the Situation Room evolved. They trace its history from early presidential inner circles and Lincoln's cabinet through Kennedy's Situation Room creation after the Bay of Pigs, Johnson's Tuesday lunches, Nixon and Kissinger, Carter, Reagan's Iran-Contra overreach, H.W. Bush's organization, and recent changes under Trump, including Steve Bannon's and McMaster's roles. They also cover the 1979 NORAD false alarm handled by Brzezinski. The episode ends with recommendations, listener mail from Emily Blasco, and sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about movies, Josh's lost glasses, and tease the episode on the National Security Council, which they say is a dry bureaucracy topic.

segments.title: What the National Security Council is for
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the NSC exists to pull together competing agencies such as State, Defense, the CIA, Energy and Treasury, so the president can weigh options, and that intelligence is decentralized and bubbles up through the hierarchy.

segments.title: Pre-NSC history and Lincoln
segments.summary: Presidents historically relied on informal inner circles. Lincoln's team of rivals, including Seward, is discussed. Congress pushed for a structured body after World War Two, leading to the National Security Act and the NSC, which Truman signed.

segments.title: How presidents used the NSC over time
segments.summary: Truman, Eisenhower (who created the National Security Advisor role and expanded the NSC), and later presidents including Obama are compared in how heavily they used the council.

segments.title: Kennedy and the origin of the Situation Room
segments.summary: After the Bay of Pigs, Kennedy and National Security Adviser McGeorge Bundy created the Situation Room in the West Wing as a place for decisions and direct access to raw intelligence. The hosts describe the room's layout and its 2006 renovation.

segments.title: Situation Room staff and daily briefings
segments.summary: The Situation Room has about thirty staff on watch teams, who compile the morning book and intelligence briefings for the president and staff, and the job is demanding and prestigious.

segments.title: Presidents' use of the NSC and the rise of the National Security Advisor
segments.summary: Presidential habits from Johnson's Tuesday lunches to Nixon and Ford's limited use are covered. Kissinger and Carter elevated the National Security Advisor's role, and Reagan's NSC overreach is noted. H.W. Bush's flow chart and committee system is treated as a model later followed.

segments.title: NSC committee structure and recent changes
segments.summary: The hosts explain the committee hierarchy from policy coordinating committees to the deputies committee and principals committee, and the NSC membership. They discuss recent changes under Trump, including Bannon's seat, its later removal, the demotion of the Joint Chiefs chairman and DNI, and H.R. McMaster's appointment. An example of a National Security Advisor's role in a 1979 NORAD false alarm is also given.

segments.title: Recommendations, listener mail, and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts recommend the documentary The Fog of War and discuss a Seymour Hersh article on the bin Laden raid, then read listener mail from Emily Blasco and sign off.
